chunks: Bakr ibn Muhammad from Juwayrah said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) passed by while I was in the Sacred Mosque waiting for a master of ours. He said, 'O Ummuthman, what keeps you here?' I said, 'I am waiting for a master of ours.' He said, 'Have you freed him?' I said, 'No.' He said, 'Have you freed his father?' I said, 'No, we freed his grandfather.' He said, 'This is not your mawla (client/slave), this is your brother.'

Therefore, there is nothing in these narrations that contradicts what we have previously stated, that the guardianship (wilayah) of the child belongs to the one who freed the father. Because what these narrations encompass is the negation of the child being a 'mawla' (in the linguistic sense of being personally freed), and that is correct because 'mawla' in language refers to the one who is personally freed, and that term is not applied to his child. And when it is negated that he is a 'mawla', it does not mean that 'wilayah' (guardianship/clientage) is also negated, because one of the two matters is distinct from the other. And that which reveals what we mentioned is what he narrated:

key_terms.الْمُعْتَقُ: Al-mu'taq (the one who has been freed)

ai.seo_question: Who inherits the wilayah (clientage) when a grandfather is freed but the father is not?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between the linguistic definition of *mawla* as the personally freed individual and the legal concept of *wilayah* (clientage), which extends to descendants when an ancestor is manumitted. This resolves the apparent contradiction by clarifying that while the grandson is not linguistically a 'mawla' himself, the legal bond of patronage still transfers to the manumitter, a nuance critical for understanding inheritance and marriage prohibitions in Shia jurisprudence. The text emphasizes that the negation of the linguistic term does not negate the legal ruling, as they are distinct categories.
